subject: literature
passage: The Dastan-e Amir Hamza, a cycle of adventure tales about the hero Hamza, was performed for centuries by professional storytellers in the cities of northern India, who could hold an audience for many evenings. In the late nineteenth century a press in Lucknow issued a printed Urdu version that ran to dozens of thick volumes. Scholar Rukhsana Mirza argues that this enormous length simply records the storytellers' practice of expanding each episode on demand to keep patrons listening; the press, in her view, set down the performers' material rather than adding new matter of its own.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Mirza's argument?

choices.A: The printed volumes were sold to readers by subscription, one volume at a time.
choices.B: Much shorter written versions of the tales had circulated in Persian for several centuries.
choices.C: Storytellers of the period are recorded as stretching a single episode over several evenings when the audience was large.
choices.D: The press's account books record payments to hired writers for composing new episodes for the printed version.

explanation.why: Mirza's argument is that the printed length came from the storytellers, not from the press adding material. A finding weakens it if it shows the press generating new content. Payments to writers for composing new episodes show exactly that.
explanation.A: Incorrect. How the volumes were sold does not show where their contents came from.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Earlier short versions in another language say nothing about whether the press added material to this one.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Storytellers stretching episodes is the practice Mirza relies on, so this would support her view.
explanation.D: Correct. If the press paid writers to compose new episodes, the printed version contains matter the press added, which Mirza denies.
